title: The Faithful and the Wicked Servant
hook: If punishment comes in 'few stripes' and 'many stripes', can it be infinite?
tldr: A steward left in charge either feeds the household or abuses it while the master is away. Matthew's wicked servant is 'cut in pieces' and placed with the hypocrites. Luke adds that servants are beaten with few or many stripes depending on what they knew. Counted, proportional stripes picture limited justice, not endless torment.
big_idea: Punishment measured in stripes is measured, and what is measured ends.

points.title: A steward over the household
points.text: The servant's job is to give the household food at the right time. The test is how he treats fellow servants while the master seems delayed.

points.title: Abuse of power is the sin
points.text: The wicked servant says 'my lord delays', beats his fellow servants and feasts with drunkards. Jesus aims this at leaders who exploit the people in their care.

points.title: 'Cut in pieces' is not literal
points.text: The rare verb means cut in two, but the servant is still alive in the next clause. Commentators read it as a severe flogging or as being cut off from the household.

points.title: With the hypocrites
points.text: In Matthew 'hypocrites' is Jesus' repeated name for scribes and Pharisees. The unfaithful servant shares the fate of the leaders Jesus denounced in the same week.

points.title: Few stripes, many stripes
points.text: Luke says the servant who knew and disobeyed gets many stripes, the one who did not know gets few. Punishment is counted and matched to knowledge.

points.title: Degrees clash with infinity
points.text: Torment that never ends is infinite for everyone, so 'few' and 'many' lose their meaning. Proportional, finite stripes fit either an end in destruction or a restoring discipline.

sections.summary: In Matthew the parable closes Jesus' answer on the Mount of Olives to the disciples' question about when the Temple would be thrown down. Jesus says 'this generation' will not pass until these things happen. Preterist readers apply much of the discourse to AD 70; others see the master's return as the second coming. Either way, the parable's demand is readiness and faithfulness now.

A master puts a servant over his household to feed them. If found faithful, he is promoted over all the master's goods. If he thinks the master is delayed, beats fellow servants and drinks with drunkards, the master returns unexpectedly, 'cuts him in pieces', and assigns him a place with the hypocrites, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth.

The Greek dichotomeo appears only here and in Luke 12:46 and means cut in two. Ellicott doubts it is literal. The Expositor's Greek Testament notes the man is still alive in the next clause, so it reads a severe thrashing. Beza and Grotius took it as dividing him from the household, dismissal. Precept Austin applies it mainly to the life to come.

Matthew places the servant with the hypocrites, the word Jesus hurls repeatedly at scribes and Pharisees in chapter 23. Luke says with the unfaithful (KJV: unbelievers). Matthew alone adds weeping and gnashing of teeth. The fate is to be classed with corrupt leaders who failed God's household, a judgment Jesus ties to that generation.

Only Luke records Peter asking whether the parable is for the disciples or for everyone. Jesus answers with the steward story, aimed at those given responsibility over others. Commentators apply it to the apostles and church leaders; in its first setting it also mirrors Israel's leaders, entrusted with God's people.

The servant who knew his master's will and did not do it is beaten with many stripes; the one who did not know but did wrong, with few. To whom much is given, much is required. The image recalls Deuteronomy 25, where a judge set the number of lashes according to the fault, with forty as the limit.

sections.h: Why proportion argues against infinite punishment
sections.summary: Traditionalists like Craig Blomberg and The Gospel Coalition use this text for degrees of punishment in hell. But if torment never ends, every sentence is infinite; as one essay puts it, anything times infinity is infinity. Rethinking Hell notes the stripes are finite by nature. Annihilationists read proportionate punishment followed by destruction; universalists read corrective discipline that ends.

visuals.title: Counting the stripes
visuals.text: And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes. But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.

objections.claim: Luke 12 proves degrees of punishment in hell, not limited punishment.
objections.strongest: Blomberg calls these verses among the clearest in the Bible for degrees of punishment in hell. Degrees can be in intensity, not duration, so eternal torment and proportional justice are compatible.
objections.response: The text speaks of counted stripes, a finite sentence set by a judge, as in Deuteronomy 25. Moving the degrees into intensity concedes that duration cannot carry them, yet an endless sentence of 'few stripes' still totals infinity. Finite, measured punishment fits conditionalism, where suffering is proportionate and then ends in destruction, or restoration, where discipline ends when it has done its work. The verse never mentions eternity.

objections.claim: Jonathan Edwards: degrees of punishment rule out annihilation, so only eternal torment fits.
objections.strongest: If the wicked are simply annihilated, everyone gets the same end: nonexistence. Only conscious, ongoing punishment can be heavier for some and lighter for others, so Luke 12 supports ECT.
objections.response: Conditionalists like Edward Fudge answer that the lost suffer in proportion to their sins before they perish; the process differs even if the end is the same. Universalists read the stripes as discipline whose length and severity fit each person. ECT is actually the view with the problem: when every sentence is unending, the difference between few and many shrinks toward nothing compared with eternity.

objections.claim: Weeping and gnashing of teeth with the hypocrites describes hell's eternal torment.
objections.strongest: Matthew 24:51 uses Jesus' recurring formula for final judgment, and the Olivet discourse leads into Matthew 25:46 and eternal punishment. Being cut asunder pictures total, final ruin.
objections.response: The servant is placed with the hypocrites, a group Jesus has just named in Matthew 23 and whose judgment he ties to 'this generation'. The cutting cannot be literal, since he lives on. Weeping and gnashing of teeth express grief and bitter frustration. Luke's parallel, the same story, explains the punishment as counted stripes, which is the opposite of infinite.
